To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the vertical distribution of turbulent kinetic energy and dissipation rate are significantly influenced by nonlocal turbulent production, which in turn is strongly influenced by stratification.
the turbulent length scale in stratified flows is limited to the Ozmidov or boundary length scale, whichever is shorter.
the turbulent length scale in stratified estuaries is limited by either the distance from the boundary or the local Ozmidov scale.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of turbulence closures to the prediction of turbulence statistics in stratified flows.
the influence of stratification and non-local turbulent production on estuarine turbulence, and the assessment of turbulence closure with field observations.
the development of turbulence closure schemes that can be used in numerical models of stratified estuarine flows.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the turbulence closure models used to parameterize the turbulent fluxes of heat and momentum in the ocean and atmosphere are inadequate for the highly stratified and weakly stratified conditions found in estuaries.
the local production–detection balance is a useful tool to describe the dynamics of turbulent motions, but that it is not a complete description of the dynamics of turbulent momentum fluxes.
the turbulence closure used here, which is the most widely used in the ocean, is not adequate to model the turbulence in this salt wedge estuary.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nonlocal turbulent momentum fluxes are significant, and the nonlocal fluxes are not adequately represented by the commonly used turbulence closures.

the local production–dissionipation balance of TKE is not a good assumption for the turbulent flow in estuaries, and that the nonlocal turbulent production and the density stratification are important factors in determining the turbulent flow.
stratification and non-local turbulent production are important factors in the closure of turbulence models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the local production–dissionipation balance is a poor approximation to the turbulent momentum flux balance under conditions of strong density stratification and/or nonlocal production.
the turbulence in estuaries is strongly influenced by both the nonlocal turbulent production associated with buoyancy-driven flows and the nonlocal dissipation associated with the stratification.
the turbulent length scale is a key variable in determining how turbulent fluxes and dissipation are distributed vertically.
